Checked against `decision_rates_{real,synthetic}.parquet` (quantity `reported A > reported B`, protocol `reported z (naive)`, strict `>`, so ties count against it).

1. **"45% and 47%": correct, but only for one setting.** It is n=120, **own search sets** (`A_vs_B_ownS`: A and B each search on their own independent S), budgets (20, 20). The synthetic number is the exact null (sigma_theta=0): 0.446 [0.422, 0.470]. The real number is the pool, all configurations: 0.4675 [0.437, 0.496]. The 74% and 57% in the same sentence are n=120 as well (synthetic ownS 0.742; real ownS 0.5695, n=60 0.566). So is the 71% (real, shared S 0.713). The sentence names neither n nor the setting, so it should. Other cells:
   - Own sets, equal budget, n=60-240: real 0.45-0.48, synthetic (sigma 0/0.01/0.03) 0.43-0.49.
   - **Shared set (`sameS`), equal budget: 0.31-0.40 real, 0.38-0.43 synthetic.** The 71% is a shared-set number, so a reader will compare it with 37% (real, n=120) and 40% (synthetic, n=120), not with 47%. The cause is ties: when A and B pick the same configuration on the same S, the reported scores are equal and `>` is false. This is not a bias in favour of B.
   Suggested wording: "at equal budgets (20 against 20, n=120, own search sets) it is 45% (synthetic) and 47% (real); on a shared set it is 40% and 37%, because ties do not count."
2. **"Within 6% up to 100 items, at most a third beyond": correct for the exhaustive search in `gap_vs_n_real`, not for every cell.** The ratio pred_kappa/gap by n:

   | n | exhaustive | random B=20 | random B=100 |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 30 | 0.95 | 0.95 | 0.94 |
   | 60 | 1.02 | 1.03 | 1.02 |
   | 100 | 1.06 | 1.09 | 1.06 |
   | 200 | 1.16 | 1.16 | 1.16 |
   | 400 | 1.26 | 1.25 | 1.26 |

   Random B=20 at n=100 is 9%. In `gap_drivers_real` (21 cells, n 60-240) the ratios run 0.93-1.32; the n=60 cells reach 1.21 and the n=240 cells 1.17-1.32. So "up to 100 items" is true of the exhaustive row only. The sentence should say "the exhaustive search", or "within 10% for n up to 100 over all searches in the gap-versus-n sweep". Each point also has a between-pool SE of 0.003-0.004 on gaps of 0.04-0.10, i.e. 4-8% of the gap, so the differences between 0.95 and 1.06 are within sampling error, and 1.16 and 1.26 are not. "By at most a third" is right for both files (max 1.32).
3. C8: still running. The first launch had died of out-of-memory within minutes (default job memory too small for the model). Relaunched at 12:57 UTC with 14 GB, 8 workers x 3 draws, about 1 h per draw, so results around 16:00-16:30 UTC. The verdict rule is the one fixed in #2 before the runs. comments.author: experiment-repo
comments.body:
Checked `paper/sections/method.tex` (dev @ 2c55526) against the code at HEAD (analysis/core.py, protocols.py, decisions.py, intervals.py, experiments/real_gap.py, run_protocols.py, assemble.py). Corrections and answers:

**Confirmed as written:** K=128 space and scoring (log-prob of each valid option letter, -inf for invalid ones, argmax; demo rows are dropped in `assemble.py`, so they are in neither S nor the truth); default config c=0; random / hill-climb / SH descriptions; κ, refined predictor, K_eff (Blom inversion of κ); optimism bootstrap (100 resamples) and .632 formulas; nested cross-fit; split and its exact (Clopper–Pearson) bound; pool-bootstrap interval with the MC variance removed.

**Corrections / precision needed**
1. *N−n ≥ 1100* holds only at n = 400 (gap-vs-n). In the protocol experiments N_tot ≤ 240, so the fresh set has ≥ 1260 items (SE ≤ 0.014). Say "N−n ≥ 1100 (n ≤ 400)" or give it per experiment. The pool is 1500 non-demo items (pool.pkl has 1512 rows, 12 demos flagged and removed): confirmed.
2. *Candidate set "evaluated" for successive halving* is the set that survives to the **last round (2 configurations)**, not all configurations ever scored (all 128 are scored in round 1, on a small subset). So max-t/Bonferroni over "evaluated" for SH is a deliberately too-narrow set; "declared" is the valid one. Say this; for random search "evaluated" = the B drawn, for hill-climb = the distinct configurations visited.
3. *Max-t lower bound*: q uses the item-level column SD of each candidate in the denominator (multiplier bootstrap, B=500 draws); the width factor is the **binomial** se of the selected configuration, sqrt(p(1−p)/n) with p(1−p) floored at 1/(4n), not an item-level se of its own. For 0/1 columns these agree except for the floor. In the decisions the same q is computed on the paired differences to the default, over the declared set.
4. *Bonferroni*: z_{1−α/m} only. The unused Šidák quantile was dead code and I removed it; the paper reports Bonferroni only. I also run `pointwise_lb` (ĉ's one-sided z bound with no multiplicity adjustment) as the unadjusted reference; add one clause naming it if you show it.
5. *Scoring on the real matrix*: "cons" = point report > fresh + 1.645·se (overstatement) or bound ≤ fresh + 1.645·se (coverage): it is the scoring more favourable to the protocol; "anticons" is against the measured fresh accuracy itself. A statement is "valid/invalid" only if both agree. Synthetic worlds have exact θ and one coverage, plus a `*_noisy` check that adds fresh-set noise to θ.
6. *Decision tests*: the naive and split tests are paired z-tests with the sample SD (ddof 1) of the per-item difference; the split test uses a 50/50 split of S. Fine as written, but "claims that tuning helped" = declared when z > 1.645.
7. *Counts*: the real protocol and decision runs will use the original pool (2000 draws of U) plus R pool-bootstrap replicates × 200 draws; R is set by the compute that is left, **not 200** as the Method says for the gap experiments. Only the gap-vs-n and C2 driver runs use 200 replicates × 100 draws plus the original pool at 2000 draws. I will give R per file in `code/results/README.md`; leave the number out of the Method until then.
8. New column for the n = 400 request from story-repo: `gap_vs_pool` (reported minus accuracy of ĉ on the whole pool, S included) next to `gap` (against pool∖S). Mean gap against pool∖S is (N/(N−n)) × the whole-pool gap for a fixed config, so the n = 400 point is 1.36× its whole-pool reading; the between-pool interval already contains this. Say in the text which one the point is.
9. *Not yet in the Method*: C7 (semi-synthetic: `analysis/semisynth.py` is in dev; its experiment runner is not yet written) and the leakage counterfactual (`experiments/matrix_facts.py`, Δ_leak; the counterfactual blocks are `cf.npz`, computed already). comments.body:
**Analysis accepts §2.1 (a), (b) and C1/C3/C4/C6/C7/C8 as written, with the amendments and fixed values below. All of this is fixed before any analysis of the matrix (only 2 of 504 matrix blocks exist, and I have looked only at pooled accuracy of the zero-shot group on 24 items in a pilot: ≈22%).**

**0. One design change you and paper need (differs from Brief v3).** Truth for the selected configuration is the accuracy on the pool items *outside S* (N−n ≈ 1300–1470 items), not a rotated 300-item fold. S is a uniform random subset of an iid pool, so pool∖S is a fresh iid sample given S: the number is unbiased for θ(ĉ), and its noise is √(p(1−p)/(N−n)) ≈ 0.013 (vs 0.03 for a 300-item block). That removes the n ≤ 200 cap: real n ∈ {30, 60, 100, 200, 400}. The 400 point is flagged: one draw is 27% of the pool, so draws overlap strongly and finite-population effects matter. The uncertainty is the same as the Brief's: the between-pool item bootstrap (resample pool items with multiplicities as weights, repeat the whole draw-search-report-truth procedure, B_boot = 200), reported as `pool-bootstrap`; spread over S draws is reported separately as `S-draw-spread`. The 12 demonstration items are outside the pool. Rule (b) stays: real-data coverage/overstatement are pairs (anti-conservative: vs Â_fresh; conservative: vs Â_fresh + 1.645·SE_fresh, SE_fresh ≈ 0.013 and computed per draw); the tolerances are restated from the synthetic arm (noisy-truth scoring run there with the same SE) before the real protocol comparison.

**1. Primary cells for C5/C6** (real matrix and synthetic/semi-synthetic arms alike): N_tot ∈ {60, 120, 240} × random search with B ∈ {20, 100}, K = 128 declared, i.e. 6 cells. C6 adds hill-climb and successive halving at N_tot = 120 and 240, B_eval matched to 100 full-S-equivalent evaluations, with candidate set = survivors / declared space. Split fractions for the split protocol: 20% and 50% reported held-out; nested CV 5-fold; optimism bootstrap n_boot = 100; Šidák/Bonferroni with m = declared K and with m = evaluated B. N_tot = 120 is the cell used for the single-number tables.

**2. Evaluated budgets for C1:** B ∈ {5, 20, 100} accepted (random search over the K = 128 grid, without replacement; B = 100 is 78% of the space, so "K_eff vs nominal K" is informative there). The exhaustive grid (B = 128) goes in a supplementary row. Hill-climb and successive halving at matched evaluations are the C3 comparison.

**3. Default/untuned configuration, fixed now:** zero-shot, "dot" option labelling, instruction wording 0 ("Choose the correct option."), cue "The answer is (" = config id 0 (group 0, variant 0). It is the first entry in each list in `src/harness.py`, chosen without reference to results. Tuned-vs-untuned also reports the gain against the unselected mean over the 128 configurations as a second reference (outline's Fig 1 reference line).

**4. Draws per cell:** 2000 draws of S on the original pool (MC SE ≤ 0.5 pp at 5%); each of the 200 bootstrap replicates uses 200 draws (cost: the real-matrix protocols are numpy on a cached matrix, but 200×2000 per cell is not affordable for the optimism bootstrap). The replicate-level MC variance is subtracted from the between-replicate variance (standard variance-component correction) before forming the pool-bootstrap interval; the uncorrected percentile interval is saved too. This is the only departure from "pool-bootstrap interval" and it is conservative if anything.

**5. C2 tolerance — amend.** The 0.01 floor would make "tracks" vacuous where the gap itself is ≈ 0.01–0.02 (large n, high σ_θ). Proposal: MAE ≤ max(0.005, 1.5 × median between-pool SE of the cell gaps, 25% of the mean measured gap); the SE term is computed from the bootstrap before the predictor is compared, so it is a precision floor, not tuned to the outcome. Primary predictor = the refined one (parametric bootstrap from shrunken θ̂, which uses the observed spread of scores); κσ̄/√n (equal-θ) is by construction an upper end and is judged as such: "holds" = measured gap ≤ predicted in ≥ 90% of cells with the between-pool interval. Both are in the file.

**6. C4 nulls.** (i) synthetic equal-θ worlds fitted to the real item-level structure; (ii) real subsets: the configurations whose full-pool accuracy lies in the densest window of width 0.02 (θ differences below the 0.013 truth noise), with the window chosen by the count of configurations it contains, not by any outcome; if fewer than 20 configurations fall in it, (ii) is dropped and said so. Rates per scenario × n ∈ {60, 120, 240} × budget ratio {1, 4} for A-vs-B.

**7. Scale contingency (new, because the matrix may disappoint).** I do not switch to a 3B model: a 2× cost on a saturated 4-CPU job queue is not affordable inside the week. If the finished matrix has mean accuracy < 0.20 or σ_θ (sampling-noise-corrected) < 0.005, this is reported in Tab 1 as the finding about this regime, C1 is then read against the noise floor as the Outline's second branch, and C7 carries the high-accuracy / high-σ_θ regimes; no configuration space is re-tuned to rescue the effect.

Compute status: the first matrix worker was killed by a memory limit (exit 137) after 2 blocks; fixed (lm-head on scored positions only, 14 GB job limit) and resubmitted; the jobs are queued behind other worlds, so matrix timing is not yet known. Synthetic-arm and protocol results do not need the matrix and will be delivered first.

# 研究任务：自动调优之后，报告的基准分数意味着什么

## 背景与动机

在大语言模型（LLM）的实际使用中，研究者常常在一个基准的题目上自动搜索提示词（prompt）
或由多个 LLM 调用组成的程序（pipeline），再把搜索得到的"最佳配置"在同一批题目上的得分
作为该系统的性能汇报。所用的自动搜索工具多种多样。

这种做法引出一个统计问题：基准题目既被用来**挑选**配置，又被用来给该配置**打分**，因此
汇报的数字不一定反映系统在全新题目上的真实表现；基于这类汇报数字做出的比较和决定是否
可靠，也就不清楚。

## 研究问题

请围绕下面的问题开展一项完整的研究：

1. 对一个先在有限题集上搜索配置、再把选出的配置拿去使用的系统，汇报的分数与它在全新
   题目上的真实表现相差多少？差距受哪些因素影响？它是否会影响基于汇报分数做出的结论？
2. 能否设计更可靠的汇报方式？应如何通过实验检验它是否可靠？

## 成功如何衡量

结论需要有你自己运行的实验支持，并至少在一个真实 LLM 与真实基准的设置上检验；实验设计、
统计工具和理论分析的深度由你决定。结论可以是支持、反驳或视条件而定。

## 关键约束

资源约束：一周墙钟时间；以 CPU 为主，涉及 LLM 推理的实验可使用至多一张 24 GB GPU 或等价
API 预算（详见 `resources.md`）；可用数据见 `data.md`；最终产出是一篇研究论文及复现代码
（详见 `deliverable.md`）。

# 研究任务：自动调优之后，报告的基准分数意味着什么

## 背景与动机

在大语言模型（LLM）的实际使用中，研究者常常在一个基准的题目上自动搜索提示词（prompt）
或由多个 LLM 调用组成的程序（pipeline），再把搜索得到的"最佳配置"在同一批题目上的得分
作为该系统的性能汇报。所用的自动搜索工具多种多样。

这种做法引出一个统计问题：基准题目既被用来**挑选**配置，又被用来给该配置**打分**，因此
汇报的数字不一定反映系统在全新题目上的真实表现；基于这类汇报数字做出的比较和决定是否
可靠，也就不清楚。

## 研究问题

请围绕下面的问题开展一项完整的研究：

1. 对一个先在有限题集上搜索配置、再把选出的配置拿去使用的系统，汇报的分数与它在全新
   题目上的真实表现相差多少？差距受哪些因素影响？它是否会影响基于汇报分数做出的结论？
2. 能否设计更可靠的汇报方式？应如何通过实验检验它是否可靠？

## 成功如何衡量

结论需要有你自己运行的实验支持，并至少在一个真实 LLM 与真实基准的设置上检验；实验设计、
统计工具和理论分析的深度由你决定。结论可以是支持、反驳或视条件而定。

## 关键约束

资源约束：一周墙钟时间；以 CPU 为主，涉及 LLM 推理的实验可使用至多一张 24 GB GPU 或等价
API 预算（详见 `resources.md`）；可用数据见 `data.md`；最终产出是一篇研究论文及复现代码
（详见 `deliverable.md`）。

# Review 2 of the idea (Brief v2, wiki revision of 2026-11-25 21:58)

Brief v2 resolves my items 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and the literature points; the compute arithmetic is now concrete and honest. Two issues remain that affect validity, one is a clarification.

1. **Pool size vs. the draw design (validity).** N ≈ 1500, verification block ≥ 2–3× the largest n, n ≤ N/4: with n_max ≈ 375 the verification block is ≈ 750–1100 and "S drawn from the rest" leaves a search remainder of only ≈ 400–750 items. S draws of size 300 from a remainder of ~500 overlap almost completely, so the many draws are not independent evidence and their spread understates between-pool variability. Block handling of SEs does not fix this: inference is conditional on one pool, and the number of effectively independent S at large n is ≈ remainder/n (1–2). Please state the inferential target explicitly (the gap *for this pool as population*, not for MMLU-Pro) and choose one of: (a) rotate the verification block (cross-fit the pool: R folds, S from the other folds) and bootstrap over items to get between-pool uncertainty; (b) cap n so that ≥ 5–10 disjoint S exist, and give the noise-floor-adjusted uncertainty; (c) say that large-n results come only from the semi-synthetic arm. 2. **Semi-synthetic extrapolation.** Larger n and K are generated from a model fitted to a 1500 × 150 matrix. Its fit can only be validated within the support of the real matrix (n ≤ 375, K ≤ 150), so extrapolation beyond that is assumption-driven. Add the check: fit on a sub-matrix (half the items/configs), predict the gap/coverage on the held-out part, and say that results beyond the real support are labelled conditional on the fitted structure.
3. (clarification) For "restrict the pool to short prompts" — this changes the population (shorter items are easier/different by subject); say what the population is then, and report the subject mix.

# Review 1 of the idea (Brief + prior_work.md @ idea-repo cf14eb0)

Overall: a strong, well-posed idea. The question matches the objective, the "known ground truth via cached item × configuration matrix" harness is the right design, the selection-vs-leakage split is a real contribution, and the conditional/negative outcome is explicitly allowed. The weaknesses are about scope vs. budget, a few under-specified estimands, and one design inconsistency. Ordered by importance; items 1–4 should change the Brief.

## What is strong
- Ground truth by construction (cached full matrix, search on S, verify on disjoint items) answers "how do we test reliability by experiment" directly (objective Q2).
- Two mechanisms separated (winner's curse over K configs vs. items-in-prompt leakage); decision-level outcomes (tuned-vs-untuned, A-vs-B, unequal budgets, CI coverage) go beyond a bias number and answer "does it affect conclusions".
- Honest prior: cites Roelofs/Recht that adaptive overfitting can be small; the Brief commits to reporting a small gap if that is what is found.
- Synthetic arm to isolate drivers and find failure regimes; real arm on MMLU-Pro as the objective requires.

## What is weak, and what would make it stronger

1. **Estimand is not fixed, so protocols cannot yet be compared "on the same terms".** The target could be (a) θ(ĉ), true accuracy of the *selected* configuration, (b) E[θ(ĉ)] / the procedure's expected performance, (c) max_c θ(c). Nested CV / cross-fit estimates (b) (Bates–Hastie–Tibshirani, which the Brief cites for exactly this), the split estimates (a) for a *different* ĉ (chosen on n−m items), the optimism bootstrap estimates (b), max-t/Šidák bound (a) from below, Ladder is about a leaderboard statistic. Scoring all of them by bias/RMSE against a single θ(ĉ) is unfair to some. Proposal: state the estimand each protocol claims, score each on its own estimand, plus one common decision-relevant yardstick (probability the reported number overstates the accuracy of the configuration actually *deployed*, and the value of a one-sided lower bound at equal coverage). Also fix the total item budget N_tot: every protocol gets the same items, a split spends items on reporting, and the final deployed configuration differs between protocols — the efficiency comparison must be at equal N_tot, as the Brief half-says.
2. **Leakage design contradicts the cache.** Demonstrations "bootstrapped from items that are then scored" depend on S, but the matrix is cached once. With demos drawn from a fixed demo pool D, "leakage" exists only when S ∩ D ≠ ∅, and its size is then set by how D is placed relative to S, not by how real tools behave (BootstrapFewShot draws demos from the search set itself). Specify: how demos are chosen, whether D ⊂ S by construction (S ⊇ D, n ≥ |D|), how the leaked cell is scored, and that leakage is a *counterfactual* quantity (score the same config on S with its demos removed from S vs. kept). Otherwise the claim "(i) decomposes the gap into selection and leakage" is not supported by the real matrix, only by the small real tool arm. The decomposition must also be reconciled with cached per-S demos at only the DSPy arm: say so and size that arm (its n, K, runs) honestly.
3. **Budget feasibility is not computed.** No GPU in this sandbox (CPU only); the Brief says "0.5–3B on CPU, K in hundreds, N in low thousands, full matrix". K=300 × N=2000 = 6e5 forward passes with few-shot prompts of hundreds to ~1.5k tokens. This is only feasible with prefix-KV reuse (one cached prefix per configuration, then ~150–250 tokens per item) and a small model. Please give the arithmetic (tokens, measured tokens/s on the actual CPU job, hours) before committing to K, N, number of models; decide in advance the fallback (smaller K, smaller N, 0.5B only) and what real-matrix claims survive. Also: a 0.5B model scores near chance on 10-option MMLU-Pro, so the spread across configurations may be dominated by letter/position bias; pick the model so accuracy is clearly above chance (≈25–40% at least) and show the per-config spread σ_θ and the pairwise item-level correlation in the real matrix, because those are the quantities that determine the gap.
4. **Search replay is limited; "matrix-replay searchers behave like real tools" needs a test.** (a) Adaptive proposal (MIPRO/GEPA/OPRO-style LLM-generated instructions) cannot be replayed on a fixed grid; the grid searchers (random, hill-climb, SH) cover "selection among given candidates", not proposal. (b) Successive halving/bandits evaluate configs on *different, nested item subsets*, so the "item × configuration matrix on S" is incomplete and a multiplier bootstrap over the evaluated set must be redefined (what is the statistic for a config scored on 40 items vs. one scored on all n?). (c) State a criterion for "behaves like": e.g. gap of the real tool arm falls within the replay searchers' predictive interval at the same n and evaluation budget — with enough tool runs to say anything (≥ a few dozen S draws).
5. **The predictor of the gap and its theory need a sharper definition.** "K_eff from the correlation of per-item outcomes" is not defined (participation ratio of the correlation matrix? count at a threshold? effective rank?), and the maximal inequality σ√(2 ln K_eff / n) is an upper bound that is often loose by a constant at moderate K; the Gaussian approximation for binary 0/1 items at accuracies in 0.3–0.5 with n of few hundred is plausible but should be checked, not assumed. The more valuable theorem-shaped object is probably: the multiplier-bootstrap max-t gives a simultaneous lower bound valid for *any* selected config in a *fixed* candidate set (Berk et al./Chernozhukov), hence also for the winner; its conservativeness (width) is then measured. Say what is proved vs. checked numerically, and keep claims at the level the checks reach.
6. **Fresh-item truth is a finite pool, and draws are dependent.** With pool N of a few thousand, "truth" on the disjoint items has sampling SD ≈ √(p(1−p)/(N−n)) ≈ 1 point at N=2000, comparable to the gap you expect; draws of S from one pool overlap more as n/N grows. This does not bias the mean gap but inflates the per-draw variance of coverage/ranking-flip indicators and makes SEs across draws too small. Define truth as pool accuracy on the complement, restrict n ≤ ~N/4 (or use all 12,032 items if the matrix cost permits, since only the verification side needs many items), report SEs with the dependence handled (e.g. a design where verification items are far more numerous than S, or sub-sampled disjoint blocks), and always report the verification-noise floor alongside the gap.
7. **Too many arms for one week; no priority order.** Eight reporting protocols, six searchers, two arms, theory, synthetic calibrated to real structure, ≥2 models if affordable. A reviewer will prefer a decisive main result to a thin sweep. Suggest: lead result = gap vs (n, K_eff, σ_θ) on the real MMLU-Pro matrix with random search, and the decision-level consequences; second = a head-to-head of the 4–5 protocols that matter (naive, split, nested CV / optimism bootstrap, Bonferroni/Šidák, max-t; Andrews hybrid and Ladder as one-sided extras); third = the DSPy arm as a short confirmatory check. Mark what is cut first when compute falls short.
8. **Decision-level claims need a null case.** The false-positive rate of "tuned beats baseline" only has meaning where the true gain is zero (or negative). The real matrix has some natural near-equal pairs but an unselected baseline config is also noisy; build explicit null scenarios (synthetic with θ equal across configs; real: subset of configs whose pool accuracies are within a tolerance), and for A-vs-B with unequal budgets say the estimand (rank by θ(ĉ_A) vs θ(ĉ_B)). Report rates with CIs and the number of draws needed to resolve a 5% vs 10% false-positive rate.
9. **Where the data have more heterogeneity than the simulator.** MMLU-Pro has 14 subjects; item difficulty and config×subject interactions are heterogeneous, which is exactly what IRT-style or Bernoulli(θ_c) simulators with a single correlation parameter miss. Calibrate the synthetic arm to the real matrix's item-level structure (low-rank/IRT fit) and test whether the predictor's error on the real matrix is within what the synthetic arm predicts.

## Literature and novelty
- **Missing and close:** Rink & Brannath, *Post-selection confidence bounds for prediction performance*, Machine Learning 2025 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-024-06632-w) treats model selection and evaluation on the *same* sample with simultaneous bounds for the selected model — very near the max-t candidate. It must be cited and the candidate positioned against it (what is new for LLM search logs: item-level matrices, correlated configs, leakage, adaptive search). Also add the classical optimism-bootstrap origin (Efron 1983; Efron & Tibshirani 1997 .632+) for that baseline, Efron's empirical-Bayes treatment of selection bias ("Tweedie's formula and selection bias", JASA 2011) for the shrinkage baseline, and prompt/option-order sensitivity of letter scoring (e.g. Zheng et al. 2024 "LLMs are not robust multiple-choice selectors"; Pezeshkpour & Hruschka 2024), because the real-matrix configuration spread comes largely from these. I have not verified the details of the last four from their text; check before citing. Hyperparameter-optimization overfitting to the validation set (e.g. Cawley–Talbot is cited; HPO-specific evidence would add to it).
- **Novelty claim wording.** "To our reading none of it characterises …" is a negative claim; keep it hedged, and re-check at each release. The objective says one published paper on this question exists; the role is barred from it, and so is this review. Novelty therefore rests on parts that are demonstrably specific to your design (decomposition with ground truth, predictor from the search log, protocol head-to-head), so the Brief should state the lead contribution as an *evidence-based answer* (size, drivers, which protocols are valid), not as "first to notice the gap", which is likely not first.
- Prior_work.md lists Varma & Simon 2006 as "to be located"; verify or drop.

## Smallest changes that raise the idea most
(1) fix an estimand per protocol and an equal total-item budget; (2) respecify leakage on the cached design; (3) put the compute arithmetic and a fallback in the Brief; (4) add the Rink–Brannath comparison; (5) a priority order of arms. I will re-review when the Brief changes and review the plan when the Outline appears.

# Review of the Outline v1 (story-repo wiki, 2026-11-25 22:07) against the objective and Brief v3

Overall: the outline carries both objective questions (C1–C4 = Q1; C5–C6 = Q2, with the real-LLM/real-benchmark requirement in C1–C2), every claim is stated as a question with a decision rule, the branches in §6 keep the story from being forced, and the paper structure is complete for the venue criteria. The weaknesses are that some decision rules are not yet decidable, the cut order contradicts the objective, and a few claims over-reach the design.

## Must change
1. **Cut order drops half of the objective.** "extras → C8 → C7 → C5 → C1–C4" puts C5 (reporting protocols) and C6 below C3 and next to cut. Objective Q2 ("can a more reliable reporting method be designed, and how is it tested by experiment") is required, not an extra, and C5/C6 run on the cached matrix and on CPU at small marginal cost once the matrix exists (the matrix is the expensive part). Proposed order of cuts: extras → C8 → C7 beyond-support extension → searcher variants inside C3 (keep random search) → protocol extras inside C5 (keep naive, split, nested CV, optimism bootstrap, Šidák, max-t). C1, C2, C4, C5 (reduced), C6 (random search + one adaptive searcher) are the floor, and the abstract is written against them. Note also C5/C6 and the synthetic arm need no LLM, so they should start in parallel with the matrix (the outline says this in §5; make the cut order consistent with it).
2. **Decision rules are not yet decidable.** "differs from nominal", "off by more than its stated tolerance", "recommended follows from the data" would let any outcome be read as support. Fix before results exist (this is a study about forking paths; it should not have them): C2 — a numerical tolerance for the predictor (e.g. absolute error ≤ the noise floor / ≤ 25% relative, or calibration slope CI containing 1) and the statistic (calibration slope, MAE); C4 — a practical margin (e.g. false-positive rate above nominal+margin, with the MC SE) and a minimum number of draws; C5 — the primary validity criterion (lower-bound coverage ≥ nominal − 2·MC SE; point report overstatement probability ≤ 50%+margin) and the primary efficiency metric at stated (n, N_tot) cells; "dominates" defined. Write these on the page now as the analysis plan and have experiment-repo accept or amend them before the matrix is analysed.
3. **C2 over-claims "explained by n, K_eff and σ_θ" from observational strata.** On the real matrix, σ_θ and K_eff cannot be set; they are read off subsets of configurations and are strongly confounded with each other and with accuracy level. The word "explained" should only be earned where they are manipulated: the semi-synthetic/synthetic arm (a factorial design) and sub-sampled real config sets. Reword C2 to "tracks" on the real matrix, and move causal wording to the factorial arm; evidence column should name the factorial design.
4. **C4 lacks its objects.** Define on the page what "untuned" is on the matrix (a fixed default configuration, which also has estimation noise but no selection), what "significance" test is applied on S (paired or unpaired, which α), and what an A-vs-B comparison with unequal budgets is estimated against (ranking by θ(ĉ_A) vs θ(ĉ_B)). Otherwise Fig 3 cannot be specified by presentation.
5. **Title and scope over-reach.** "prompt and pipeline search" — the design covers instruction/format/demonstration configurations of a single call, scored by letter log-probs of one ≈1.5B model on one benchmark. No multi-stage pipelines and no generative/sampled outputs. Title and abstract should say "prompt/configuration search" (or add "pipeline" only if C8 delivers a pipeline), and §7 must state the generative/CoT gap as a limitation, not only model scale.

## Should change
6. **Name the proposed protocol.** Q2 asks for a more reliable reporting method; the outline treats six protocols symmetrically and says the recommendation follows from the data. That is fine for honesty but weak as a contribution. State the *candidate* up front (max-t on the logged item-level matrix with a declared candidate set, with the split and nested CV as the controls it must beat or match on stated criteria), and add a "what to log and report" recipe (table or boxed text) as a practitioner-usable output of C5/C6; if the candidate fails, the paper says so.
7. **C1 needs the search budget stated.** The gap depends on the number of configurations actually *evaluated* (B), not only K of the declared space; list B in the experiments (e.g. B ∈ {5, 20, 100} of K≈100–150) and in Fig 1/2 axes. Also state the number of real n values and disjoint S so the power of "CI includes 0" is known: with noise floor ≈0.03 per rotation and ~30 disjoint S, say what gap size is detectable.
8. **Fig 1** should show, next to the naive-vs-fresh curve, the untuned/default configuration's fresh accuracy and the *unselected* random-configuration mean (so the reader sees the tuned gain and the optimism on the same axis). Otherwise the headline cannot show whether the optimism matters relative to the gain from tuning, which is the decision-relevant comparison.
9. **C8 and C7 as titled claims.** C8 "shows a gap consistent with matrix replay" presupposes the result; word as "does the real-tool gap fall within the replay interval" (it is, in §2's rule, but the claim cell reads as an expected outcome). Same for C6's "valid for a fixed declared candidate set" — that is proved/standard, the tested question is the adaptive failure; keep as written in the Decision column.
10. **Related work ordering/novelty.** Keep the hedge; put Rink–Brannath in the intro's what-is-known sentence too, since a reviewer who knows it will look for it early. §2 Intro "selection-bias theory exists but not for searched LLM configurations" is a negative claim: say "to our reading".

## Checked and fine
- Structure vs the objective's required sections and the venue criteria; contributions as evidence-based answers; branches in §6; honest null handling; the requests to other roles (matrix first; presentation tells when a claim cannot be shown).
- Figure set is one claim per figure; Tab 1 carries the matrix facts (σ_θ, correlation, letter-bias share, compute) that determine the gap, as I asked of the idea.

I will re-review when the Outline changes (and when results revise claims) if you reopen or mention this issue; items 1–5 are the ones I would not leave out of v2.

# 研究任务：自动调优之后，报告的基准分数意味着什么

## 背景与动机

在大语言模型（LLM）的实际使用中，研究者常常在一个基准的题目上自动搜索提示词（prompt）
或由多个 LLM 调用组成的程序（pipeline），再把搜索得到的"最佳配置"在同一批题目上的得分
作为该系统的性能汇报。所用的自动搜索工具多种多样。

这种做法引出一个统计问题：基准题目既被用来**挑选**配置，又被用来给该配置**打分**，因此
汇报的数字不一定反映系统在全新题目上的真实表现；基于这类汇报数字做出的比较和决定是否
可靠，也就不清楚。

## 研究问题

请围绕下面的问题开展一项完整的研究：

1. 对一个先在有限题集上搜索配置、再把选出的配置拿去使用的系统，汇报的分数与它在全新
   题目上的真实表现相差多少？差距受哪些因素影响？它是否会影响基于汇报分数做出的结论？
2. 能否设计更可靠的汇报方式？应如何通过实验检验它是否可靠？

## 成功如何衡量

结论需要有你自己运行的实验支持，并至少在一个真实 LLM 与真实基准的设置上检验；实验设计、
统计工具和理论分析的深度由你决定。结论可以是支持、反驳或视条件而定。

## 关键约束

资源约束：一周墙钟时间；以 CPU 为主，涉及 LLM 推理的实验可使用至多一张 24 GB GPU 或等价
API 预算（详见 `resources.md`）；可用数据见 `data.md`；最终产出是一篇研究论文及复现代码
（详见 `deliverable.md`）。

issue.author: idea-review-repo
issue.body:
Review of Outline v3 (89bcef9). The §2.2 amendments are sound: truth = pool∖S (noise 0.013) is a cleaner estimand than the rotated block, since S is a uniform subset of an iid pool and pool∖S is fresh given S. The n = 400 flag, the scale contingency, and the fixed default configuration are all good. Two rule-level points remain; neither blocks.

1. **C2 "tracks" can pass because the data are noisy.** The tolerance is max(0.005, 1.5 × median between-pool SE, 25% of the mean gap), and the slope-CI-contains-1 test is also easiest to pass when the CI is wide. If the SE term sets the max, "tracks" says only "consistent with the predictor", not that the predictor discriminates. Suggest stating in the rule which term set the tolerance in the delivered result, and wording the outcome "consistent with, not discriminating" when the SE term dominates or the slope CI is wider than a stated width (for example, containing 0 as well as 1). A reader can then tell a tracked gap from an unmeasured one.

2. **C4 real-matrix null (ii) is a near-null, not a null.** Configurations within a 0.02 window of full-pool accuracy can differ in true θ by up to 0.02. At n = 240 that is within the tests' power, so a measured A-vs-B flip rate or tuned-vs-untuned rate there mixes selection error with real differences. Suggest that "above nominal" (the 1 pp rule) be judged on the synthetic equal-θ worlds (i), and that real (ii) be reported as near-null, with the pool-accuracy spread inside the window reported beside each rate. Otherwise a rate above nominal on (ii) cannot be separated from a genuine difference.

# Review of Outline v2: items 1–10 are resolved; two rule-level gaps remain

v2 takes my ten points well (cut order, pre-specified rules in §2.1, "tracks" vs "explained", C4 objects, scope words, Box 1). I would approve the plan as it stands apart from the two statistical points below, which sit in §2.1 and decide whether C4/C5/C6 can be read at all.

1. **Coverage is scored against a noisy truth.** C5/C6 validity = "lower-bound coverage ≥ 0.95 − 2·MC SE" and C5's point-report "P(report > θ(ĉ_deployed))". θ(ĉ) is only observed as accuracy on a ≈300-item verification fold (noise ≈ 0.03, as large as the gap). For a bound that is tight (L close to θ) the event "L ≤ verification accuracy" is not the event "L ≤ θ": a valid bound can look under-covering, a conservative one over-covering, and P(report > θ) drifts toward 0.5 as the noise grows relative to the gap. Add to §2.1 how truth enters: either score against a verification-noise-corrected quantity (e.g. check L ≤ Â_ver + z·SE_ver as a conservative test and L ≤ Â_ver as an anti-conservative one, report both), or simulate the same scoring on the synthetic arm where θ is exact, to show how much the verification noise biases each criterion, and state the criterion's tolerance accordingly. Without this the §2.1 thresholds (e.g. [0.5 ± 0.05], 0.95 − 2·MC SE) are not interpretable on the real matrix.
2. **"MC SE" and "draws" are not binomial here.** C4 asks for ≥2000 draws per cell to reach SE 0.5 pp, and C5/C6 use 2·MC SE. Draws of S overlap heavily (≈6 disjoint S per rotation, 30 in total at n=200, fewer at 300), so the binomial SE of 2000 draws is the SE of the *pool-conditional* rate only; the interval on a rate that claims anything about the benchmark behaviour is the between-pool bootstrap one. Say in §2.1 which interval each rule uses ("above nominal" = the between-pool bootstrap interval excludes nominal + 1 pp, not the binomial interval), and that the 2000 draws buy precision on the pool-conditional rate only. Otherwise C4 can read "above nominal" from a narrow interval that the bootstrap would widen past the margin.

Smaller: in C1's rule, "minus nothing (the verification noise is zero-mean …)" is unclear; write "the gap is not corrected for verification noise, which has zero mean and only widens the interval." Everything else — Fig 1 reference lines, floor, branches, requests to other roles — I find sound.

comments.body: Both points taken in Outline §2.1: general rule (a) says which interval each rule uses (between-pool bootstrap; draws size pool-conditional precision only); rule (b) scores coverage/overstatement on real data as an anti-conservative/conservative pair, with exact-θ synthetic arms setting the thresholds before the real matrix is analysed. C1 wording fixed.

# 研究任务：自动调优之后，报告的基准分数意味着什么

## 背景与动机

在大语言模型（LLM）的实际使用中，研究者常常在一个基准的题目上自动搜索提示词（prompt）
或由多个 LLM 调用组成的程序（pipeline），再把搜索得到的"最佳配置"在同一批题目上的得分
作为该系统的性能汇报。所用的自动搜索工具多种多样。

这种做法引出一个统计问题：基准题目既被用来**挑选**配置，又被用来给该配置**打分**，因此
汇报的数字不一定反映系统在全新题目上的真实表现；基于这类汇报数字做出的比较和决定是否
可靠，也就不清楚。

## 研究问题

请围绕下面的问题开展一项完整的研究：

1. 对一个先在有限题集上搜索配置、再把选出的配置拿去使用的系统，汇报的分数与它在全新
   题目上的真实表现相差多少？差距受哪些因素影响？它是否会影响基于汇报分数做出的结论？
2. 能否设计更可靠的汇报方式？应如何通过实验检验它是否可靠？

## 成功如何衡量

结论需要有你自己运行的实验支持，并至少在一个真实 LLM 与真实基准的设置上检验；实验设计、
统计工具和理论分析的深度由你决定。结论可以是支持、反驳或视条件而定。

## 关键约束

资源约束：一周墙钟时间；以 CPU 为主，涉及 LLM 推理的实验可使用至多一张 24 GB GPU 或等价
API 预算（详见 `resources.md`）；可用数据见 `data.md`；最终产出是一篇研究论文及复现代码
（详见 `deliverable.md`）。
